why_how.text: Registration permits road use while the title proves ownership, so an owner needs both.
Registering requires a set list of proofs on form MV-eighty-two.

scenario.text: Carlos moves to New York from another state, bringing his car.

reasoning.text: New residents must register within thirty days, and registration needs ownership proof, insurance, paid sales tax and form MV-eighty-two.

result.text: Carlos gathers his proofs and registers within thirty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the registration proves you own the car.

correction.text: Registration grants road permission, while the title proves ownership.

memory_support.text: Registration drives, title owns, thirty days for newcomers.

prompt.text: A friend who just moved here asks how long she has to register her car. What do you tell her?

rationale.text: New residents must register within thirty days; there is no matching title deadline.

title.text: Owning a car in New York

narration.text: This lesson opens the chapter on owning a vehicle. The manual starts by separating two documents that people often confuse: the registration and the title. Each has its own job, its own age rule, and its own deadline for new residents. Then we look at what you need to register a vehicle, what you receive when you do, and how a registered dealer can handle registration for you. We finish with the two insurance identification cards that your insurer issues. By the end you will know which document does what and what to bring when you register a vehicle.

lines.text: Register at sixteen; title at any age.

narration.text: Registration and title do different jobs. Registration permits you to use the vehicle on the road. The title proves that you own it. The age rules differ too: you must be at least sixteen to register a vehicle, but you can title one at any age. And new residents must register their vehicles within thirty days. So a teenager under sixteen could own a car through its title, but could not register it. And someone moving to New York has thirty days to get the registration done. Keep the two documents separate in your mind, because each answers a different question.

lines.text: New residents register within thirty days.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People treat registration and title as the same thing, or think registration proves ownership. The manual is precise. Registration grants road permission, while the title proves ownership. And new residents face a thirty-day registration clock. So if a question asks which document proves who owns the car, the answer is the title. If it asks which document lets the car be driven on the road, the answer is the registration. And the thirty-day deadline for new residents belongs to registration, not to the title.

To register a vehicle you need proof of ownership or the owner's authorization, insurance, and paid sales taxes. You also need odometer and damage statements, and you file it all on form MV-eighty-two, with six-point proof of your name and birth date, following guide MV-eighty-two point one. When you register, you receive plates, a registration document and a sticker. For a vehicle bought from someone other than a dealer, you can request a ten-day inspection extension. A car bought from a dealer must already carry an inspection from within thirty days.

lines.text: Dealers may register for the buyer.
Two insurance cards that must match.

narration.text: A registered dealer may register the car for the buyer, with temporary paperwork and plates, for a processing fee plus the state fees. That can save you a trip. Your insurer, meanwhile, issues two insurance identification cards. The names and the VIN on them must match the registration application exactly. You present one card when you register, and you keep the other one in the car. So when you register, check the cards carefully, because a mismatch in the name or the VIN means they do not match the application as the manual requires.

Here is a quick check: a friend who just moved to New York asks how long she has to register her car here. What do you tell her? Work it out before reading on. The answer is thirty days. New residents must register within thirty days. Remember too that registration permits road use while the title proves ownership. And when she registers, she will need ownership proof, insurance, paid sales tax and the odometer and damage statements on form MV-eighty-two, with name and birth-date proof.

lines.text: Registration for the road; title for ownership.
Bring proofs; keep one insurance card in the car.

narration.text: To close, registration permits road use while the title proves ownership, registration needs age sixteen while titling has no age limit, and new residents must register within thirty days. Registering demands ownership or owner authorization, insurance, paid sales taxes, and odometer and damage statements on form MV-eighty-two with six-point name and birth-date proof, and it yields plates, a document and a sticker. Registered dealers may register the car for you with temporary paperwork and plates. Insurers issue two matching cards, one for registration and one for the car. Next we look at ownership papers.

why_how.text: The ownership papers you need depend on who sold you the car.
Checking the title protects you from liens, rejected titles and hidden damage history.

scenario.text: Mia is buying a used car from a private seller.

reasoning.text: Private-used purchases need the signed-over title, and buyers check it for lien holders before accepting it.

result.text: Mia checks the title face for liens, sees none, and accepts the signed-over title.

claim.text: Common mistake: accepting a title without checking it for a lien holder.

correction.text: Buyers check the title face for lien holders, demand a lender release, or risk repossession by the lien holder.

memory_support.text: Check liens, check statements, nine for damage, ten for odometer.

prompt.text: You are about to accept a title from a seller. What do you look for on its face?

answer.text: Lien holders showing unpaid vehicle loans.

rationale.text: If there is a lien, demand a lender release, or the lien holder could repossess the car.

lines.text: Papers for each kind of sale.
Checking a title before you accept it.

narration.text: This lesson is about the paperwork that proves ownership when you buy a vehicle. The papers differ depending on whether you buy new or used, from a dealer or from a private seller. Then we look at how to check a title before you accept it: for lien holders, for missing or altered statements, and for the odometer and damage disclosures that depend on the vehicle's age. We finish with vehicles branded Rebuilt Salvage, which need an extra examination. Careful checking at this stage protects you from problems that are hard to fix later.

lines.text: Dealer new: origin certificate plus MV-fifty.
Dealer used: prior title plus MV-fifty.

narration.text: The ownership papers depend on the sale. A new car from a dealer comes with a manufacturer's certificate of origin plus an MV-fifty certificate of sale. A used car from a dealer comes with the prior title, form MV-nine hundred ninety-nine, with odometer and salvage statements, plus the MV-fifty. A dealer who does not register the car must still hand over those papers with a signed MV-eighty-two. A used car from an out-of-state dealer needs a signed-over title or transferable registration with a bill and proofs. And a private used car needs the signed-over title, or a transferable registration for nineteen seventy-two and older.

lines.text: Dealer: origin or title plus MV-fifty.
Only dealers can skip your MV-eighty-two trip.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Buyers sometimes expect the same paperwork from every seller. The manual contrasts them. Dealer sales pair origin or title papers with an MV-fifty, while private sales lean on the signed-over title alone. And only dealer paperwork can skip the buyer's own MV-eighty-two trip. So from a private seller, you will not get an MV-fifty, and you will file your own MV-eighty-two. From a dealer, you get the MV-fifty with the origin or title papers, and the dealer's paperwork may save you the trip. Ask yourself first who the seller is, then which papers to expect.

lines.text: Look for lien holders on the title.

narration.text: Before you accept any title, check its face for lien holders. A lien holder listed there shows an unpaid vehicle loan. If you see one, demand a release from the lender. If you do not, you risk the lien holder repossessing the car. So this check is the first thing to do with any title a seller hands you. Reading the face of the title is the check, and a lender release is the fix when a lien appears. A clean title face, or a lender release for any lien, is what you want to see before you accept it. So the order is simple: read the face, look for a lien holder, and get the lender release before you accept the title.

lines.text: Eight years or newer: both statements.
Ten or newer: odometer on the title back.
Nine and older: no damage disclosure.

narration.text: Disclosure rules depend on the vehicle's age. Cars eight model years old or newer need both seller-completed and buyer-signed odometer and damage statements, and the damage statement may brand the new title Rebuilt Salvage. Cars ten model years old or newer need the odometer statement on the back of the title, while damage disclosure drops off at nine model years and older. The buyer initials the odometer box and matches it to the reading on the dashboard. So the age of the car tells you which statements must be there, and the dash reading is your check.

lines.text: Damage disclosure ends at nine model years.

narration.text: Here is a second trap. The two disclosure cutoffs are one year apart, and the manual itself calls them an off-by-one pair that traps skimmers. Damage disclosure dies at nine model years, while odometer disclosure survives to ten. So a car that is nine model years old no longer needs a damage disclosure, but it still needs the odometer statement. If a question asks which disclosure lasts longer, the answer is the odometer statement. Read model-year questions slowly, because swapping nine and ten is exactly the mistake the manual warns about.

lines.text: You are about to accept a title.
What do you look for first?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a seller hands you the title to a used car you are buying. What do you look for on its face before accepting it? Work it out before reading on. The answer is lien holders, which show unpaid vehicle loans. If one is listed, demand a release from the lender, or you risk the lien holder repossessing the car. Then check that the odometer and damage statements are completed and that nothing is altered, erased or cancelled, because offices reject titles with those problems. A Rebuilt Salvage vehicle also needs a stolen-parts examination.

To close, dealer-new ownership is a manufacturer origin certificate plus an MV-fifty, dealer-used is the prior title with odometer and salvage statements plus an MV-fifty, and private-used needs the signed-over title, or a transferable registration for nineteen seventy-two and older. Before accepting a title, check its face for lien holders and demand a lender release. Offices reject titles lacking completed odometer or damage statements or showing alterations, erasures or cancellations. Damage disclosure drops off at nine model years and odometer disclosure at ten. Rebuilt Salvage vehicles need a stolen-parts examination. Next comes sales tax.

why_how.text: Who collects sales tax depends on whether you buy from a dealer.
Plate refunds and plate removal protect your money and your record.

scenario.text: Nadia buys a car from a neighbor for less than its market value.

reasoning.text: Non-dealer sales trigger form DTF-eight hundred two with buyer-completed price certification and a seller signature when the price trails market value.

result.text: Nadia and the neighbor complete the form, or the tax will default to market value.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a private sale avoids sales tax.

correction.text: Non-dealer sales use form DTF-eight hundred two, defaulting otherwise to market-value tax at registration.

memory_support.text: Dealer collects, private files, plates off before you sell.

prompt.text: You sold your car to a stranger yesterday. What should you have removed before handing it over?

answer.text: The plates and the windshield sticker.

rationale.text: Otherwise the stranger's parking tickets may be billed to you as the old owner.

lines.text: Sales tax by kind of seller.

narration.text: This lesson covers the money side of owning a vehicle. First, sales tax: who collects it when you buy from a dealer, and what form you use when you buy from someone else. Then registration fees and refunds: how long most registrations run, how fees are figured, and what you get back when you return plates. Finally, a simple habit that protects you when you sell or trade a car: taking the plates and the windshield sticker off first. Each of these rules has a reason stated in the manual, and knowing the reason makes the rule easier to remember.

lines.text: Other sellers: form DTF-eight hundred two.

narration.text: Registered dealers collect sales tax directly as part of the sale. When you buy from anyone else, form DTF-eight hundred two comes into play. The buyer completes the price certification, and the seller signs it, when the price is below market value or the car is a gift from someone outside the family. Otherwise the tax defaults to market value at registration. So in a private sale, the form is how you show the actual price. Without it, the office charges tax on the market value, whatever you actually paid for the car.

lines.text: Dealer: tax built into the deal.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People assume a private sale either has no tax or is taxed on the price they say they paid. The manual says dealer purchases bake sales tax into the deal, while private buys file DTF-eight hundred two. And a missing seller signature defaults the tax to market value rather than the claimed price. So if you buy privately below market value, the seller's signature on the form matters. Without it, you pay tax on market value. With a dealer, the tax is simply part of the purchase, and there is no separate form for you to file.

lines.text: Most run two years, weight-based fees.
Unused plates back in sixty days: full refund.

narration.text: Most registrations for vehicles up to eighteen thousand pounds run two years, with fees based on weight plus plate and title fees. Refunds follow clear rules. If the plates were used, there is no refund. If unused plates are returned within sixty days, you get a full refund minus processing. If only the first year was used, the second-year fees are refunded. Plate turn-ins need a receipt, form FS-6T. And transfer credit follows only the replacement vehicle. So keep the receipt when you return plates, because it is the record of the turn-in.

lines.text: Or a stranger's tickets may bill you.

narration.text: When you sell or trade a vehicle, remove the plates and the windshield sticker first. The manual gives the reason plainly: if you do not, parking tickets run up by a stranger may be billed to you as the old owner. So the plates and sticker stay with you, not with the car. Combine this with the refund rules from the last slide: plates you return unused within sixty days get a full refund minus processing, but plates that were used get none. Either way, the plates should leave the car with you on the day you hand it over to the new owner.

Here is a quick check: you sold your car to a stranger yesterday. What should you have removed before handing it over? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the plates and the windshield sticker. If they stay on the car, the stranger's parking tickets may be billed to you as the old owner. Returning the plates is also how a refund works: unused plates returned within sixty days refund fully minus processing, while used plates bring no refund. And remember the private sale's tax form, DTF-eight hundred two, which the buyer completes and the seller signs.

lines.text: Dealers collect tax; private sales file.

narration.text: To wrap up, registered dealers collect sales tax directly, while other sellers trigger form DTF-eight hundred two, with buyer-completed price certification and a seller signature when the price trails market value or the car is a non-family gift, defaulting otherwise to market-value tax at registration. Most registrations to eighteen thousand pounds run two years on weight-based fees. Used plates kill any refund, unused plates returned within sixty days refund fully minus processing, and turn-ins need receipt FS-6T. Strip the plates and sticker before selling. Next we look at renewing a registration.

why_how.text: Registrations renew every two years, and the owner must plan for processing time.
Mail, online and in-person renewal each have their own requirements.
Expiries on weekends or state holidays stretch to midnight of the next business day.

scenario.text: Ray recently moved and wants to renew his registration online.

reasoning.text: Online renewal fits only unchanged addresses and carriers.

result.text: Ray renews by mail with a separate note for his new mailing address, or uses MV-two hundred thirty-two to change every record.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking online renewal works even after an address change.

correction.text: Online renewal forbids any address or carrier change, while mail renewal tolerates address changes with a side note.

memory_support.text: Mail allows a note, online allows no change, office needs a signature.

prompt.text: Your registration expires on a Saturday. Until when is it good?

answer.text: Until midnight of the next business day, with insurance kept up.

rationale.text: Weekend and holiday expiries stretch automatically to midnight of the next business day.

narration.text: This lesson covers renewing your registration. The manual explains the two-year renewal cycle, when reminders arrive and why you might not receive one, and what happens when an expiry date falls on a weekend or holiday. Then it describes three ways to renew: by mail, online, and in person. Each path has its own requirements, and the differences are a common source of confusion, so we will compare them side by side. By the end you should be able to pick the right renewal path for your own situation and know what each one asks of you.

lines.text: Reminders forty-five to sixty days out.

narration.text: Registrations renew every two years. The DMV mails a reminder forty-five to sixty days before the expiry date. You may not get one if your address on file has lapsed, if three or more parking tickets stand unanswered, or if your credentials are suspended. Processing takes about two weeks, and the manual says the owner must anticipate that time, with no excuse for missing it. So do not count on the reminder alone. Know your expiry date, and renew early enough that the two weeks of processing finish before the registration runs out.

lines.text: Expiry on a weekend or state holiday.
Stretches to the next business day.

narration.text: If your registration expires on a weekend or a state holiday, the expiry stretches automatically to midnight of the next business day. Your insurance must be maintained throughout that time. So a registration that would expire on a Saturday is still good until midnight the following Monday, if Monday is a business day. The stretch depends on your insurance staying in force the whole time, because the registered vehicle must stay insured whether it is driven or parked. So a weekend or holiday expiry gives you until midnight of the next business day, and no longer.

lines.text: Mail: MV-eighty-two, a check, a note.
MV-two hundred thirty-two changes every record.
Online: no address or carrier change.

narration.text: To renew by mail, file form MV-eighty-two, with a separate note if you want an alternate mailing address, because an address written on the MV-eighty-two joins only that record, while form MV-two hundred thirty-two alone changes every record. Include a check to the Commissioner, with the fee from MV-204A, and an insurance card if your carrier changed. Send it to the Utica processing center and allow two weeks, longer from overseas. Name changes need an office visit. Online renewal fits passenger cars, small trucks and some motorcycles when the address and carrier are unchanged.

lines.text: File MV-eighty-two with the registrant's signature.
Second parties show their own original ID.
Plus original or copy for the registrant.

narration.text: To renew in person, file form MV-eighty-two with the registrant's signature. If someone else does the renewal for the registrant, including a spouse, that person must show their own original identification, plus an original or a copy of identification for the registrant. So a husband renewing his wife's registration brings his own original identification and hers, along with the form she has signed. Online renewal, by contrast, shows the fees on screen and takes a credit card in three steps, with the registration mailed within two weeks, but only when nothing has changed.

lines.text: Mail: address change with a side note.
Online: no address or carrier change.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People assume all three renewal paths accept the same situations. The manual separates them. Mail renewal tolerates address changes with a side note. Online renewal forbids any address or carrier change. And office visits demand the registrant's own signature, even when a proxy brings the form. So if you have moved, online renewal is not for you, but mail renewal with a note is. If someone else is going to the office for you, you still sign the form. Match your situation to the path before you start, so the renewal is not turned back.

Here is a quick check: your registration expires on a Saturday, and the offices are closed for the weekend. Until when is it good? Work it out before reading on. The answer is until midnight of the next business day, as long as your insurance is maintained throughout. Expiries that land on weekends or state holidays stretch automatically. That rule does not replace planning, though. Renewals run every two years, reminders come forty-five to sixty days out, and the owner must allow about two weeks of processing, without excuse for missing the deadline.

lines.text: Every two years; plan for processing.
Weekend expiries stretch a day or two.

narration.text: To close, renewals run every two years with mailed reminders forty-five to sixty days out, which can be lost through a lapsed address, three or more unanswered parking tickets or suspended credentials, and the owner must allow two weeks of processing. Weekend and holiday expiries stretch to midnight of the next business day with insurance maintained. Mail renewal uses MV-eighty-two with a side note for another address. Online renewal needs unchanged addresses and carriers. In-person renewal needs the registrant's signature, and second parties show identification for both. Next comes insurance.

why_how.text: A registered vehicle must stay liability-insured whether driven or parked.
Lapses and uninsured driving carry penalties up to revocation.
Minimum coverage is set per incident for death, injury and property.

scenario.text: Pat's insurance is about to end because she is selling the car next month.

reasoning.text: Before coverage lapses, plates go back with a receipt, or daily civil penalties or registration suspension follow.

result.text: Pat returns the plates before the coverage ends and keeps the receipt.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a car that sits parked does not need insurance.

correction.text: A registered vehicle must stay liability-insured whether driven or parked.

memory_support.text: Fifty and a hundred for death, twenty-five and fifty for injury, ten for property.

prompt.text: What is the minimum coverage for property damage?

rationale.text: Death runs fifty and one hundred thousand, injury twenty-five and fifty thousand, and property ten thousand.

narration.text: This lesson covers the insurance you must carry. The manual says a registered vehicle must stay insured whether it is driven or parked. Then it sets minimum coverage amounts for death, injury and property. It explains what to do before your coverage lapses, the one vehicle type that is treated differently, and the penalties for driving uninsured. Because the minimums come in pairs of numbers, they are easy to mix up, so we will look at the pattern that ties them together. By the end you will know what coverage you need and what to do if it is about to end.

The basic rule is short. A registered vehicle must stay liability-insured whether it is driven or parked. So a car sitting in a garage for the winter, if it is still registered, still needs insurance. There is no gap allowed just because the car is not being used. This rule ties into the renewal rules from the last lesson, where even a weekend expiry extension depends on insurance being maintained. If you truly want to stop insuring a car, the manual's answer is on the next slides: the plates go back first, before the coverage lapses.

lines.text: Death: fifty thousand, one hundred thousand.

narration.text: The minimum liability coverage is set per incident. For death, it is fifty thousand dollars for one person and one hundred thousand dollars for two or more. For injury, it is twenty-five thousand dollars for one person and fifty thousand dollars for two or more. For property, it is ten thousand dollars. So there are five numbers to remember: fifty and one hundred for death, twenty-five and fifty for injury, and ten for property. Each figure is per incident. Saying them in that order, death, then injury, then property, helps keep them in their right places.

lines.text: Each death figure doubles its injury figure.

narration.text: Here is the trap. With five numbers, people swap the death and injury minimums. The manual gives a pattern that settles it. Death minimums run fifty and one hundred thousand, while injury runs twenty-five and fifty, with ten for property, so death always doubles injury at each headcount. For one person, injury is twenty-five and death is fifty. For two or more, injury is fifty and death is one hundred. So if you remember the injury figures, double them to get death. And property stands alone at ten thousand. Notice that fifty appears twice, once for each, with a different headcount.

lines.text: Return plates with an FS-6T receipt.
Ninety uninsured days: license suspended too.

narration.text: If your coverage is going to lapse, return the plates first and get an FS-6T receipt. Otherwise daily civil penalties or a registration suspension follow. If the vehicle goes ninety days uninsured without the plates returned, your driver license is suspended too. If the DMV sends you a letter about insurance, you must answer it. Motorcycles are the exception: they skip the plate turn-in. The manual describes that motorcycle exception as the chapter's cleanest exception to a universal rule, since motorcycles must carry insurance like cars yet skip the plate turn-in on lapse.

lines.text: Everyone driving or lending must be insured.
At least one year of revocation.

narration.text: Everyone who drives or lends a car in the state, whether a resident or not, must prove acceptable insurance. Driving uninsured, lending an uninsured car, or crashing while uninsured revokes the license for at least one year. So the duty does not stop at the owner. Lending your uninsured car to a friend is covered, and so is a visitor from another state driving here. The penalty is serious: revocation, not just a fine, and for at least a year. Combined with the rule that a registered vehicle stays insured even while parked, there is no situation where a registered car may go uninsured.

Here is a quick check: what is the minimum liability coverage for property damage? Work it out before reading on. The answer is ten thousand dollars per incident. The other minimums are fifty thousand dollars for one death and one hundred thousand for two or more, and twenty-five thousand for one injury and fifty thousand for two or more. Remember the pattern: at each headcount, the death minimum doubles the injury minimum. If you answered twenty-five thousand, that is the minimum for injury to one person, not the property minimum.

To wrap up, a registered vehicle must stay liability-insured whether driven or parked. The minimums are fifty thousand for one death and one hundred thousand for two or more, twenty-five thousand for one injury and fifty thousand for two or more, and ten thousand for property, all per incident, so death doubles injury at each headcount. Before coverage lapses, plates go back with an FS-6T receipt, or penalties or suspension follow, and ninety uninsured days suspend the license too. Motorcycles skip the plate turn-in. Uninsured driving, lending or crashing revokes at least one year. Next comes inspection.

why_how.text: Inspection deadlines depend on how you bought the vehicle.
The DMV licenses dealers, stations and repair shops, so buyers have a complaint path.

scenario.text: Ana buys a used car from a private seller and registers it.

reasoning.text: Non-dealer buys need inspection within ten days of registration, with a VS-one thousand seventy-seven extension on request.

result.text: Ana books an inspection within ten days of registering.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every buyer gets the same thirty days to inspect.

correction.text: Dealer-bought cars get thirty inspection days, private buys get ten after registration, and movers keep an old certificate up to a year.

memory_support.text: Thirty for dealer buys, ten for private, a year for movers.

prompt.text: You moved to New York with a car whose inspection certificate is still current. How long does it last?

answer.text: To its expiry or one year, whichever comes first.

rationale.text: Movers keep an old certificate up to a year, while dealer buys get thirty days and private buys ten.

narration.text: This lesson covers vehicle inspection and how to protect yourself as a consumer. The manual sets inspection deadlines that depend on how you got the vehicle: from an in-state dealer, from a private seller, or as a new resident moving in. It lists transfers that are exempt, explains when re-inspection is due and where to go, what happens after you pass or fail, and how emissions and diesel inspections work. Finally, it explains that the DMV licenses dealers, stations and repair shops, and how to complain if something goes wrong. There is a lot here, so we will take it step by step.

lines.text: In-state sale: within thirty days, before delivery.
Private buy: ten days after registration.
Mover: keep the certificate up to a year.

narration.text: Vehicles sold in the state need an inspection within thirty days, with a certificate before delivery. If you buy from someone other than a dealer, the vehicle needs inspection within ten days of registration, and you can request an extension on form VS-one thousand seventy-seven. If you move here with a vehicle that already has an inspection certificate, it remains valid until it expires or for one year, whichever comes first. Some retail transfers are exempt: welfare-to-work transfers, chassis transfers, factory-direct delivery, out-of-state or country registration, scrap, and lease buyouts.

lines.text: Private buy: ten days after registration.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People assume one inspection deadline fits every buyer. The manual sets three clocks for three buyer kinds. Dealer-bought cars enjoy thirty inspection days. Private buys get ten days after registration. And movers keep an old certificate up to a year. So the question to ask is how you got the car. From an in-state dealer, thirty days. From a private seller, ten days once you register. Moving in with a current certificate, it lasts until expiry or one year, whichever comes first. Do not let the thirty-day dealer figure stand in for the shorter private-sale deadline.

lines.text: Use the right kind of station.

narration.text: After the first inspection, re-inspection falls due before the current certificate expires and whenever the registrant changes. Inspections are done at yellow-and-black inspection stations. Heavy trucks, buses, tractors and trailers go to heavy-vehicle stations, and motorcycles go to motorcycle stations. Signing a renewal certifies that the inspection is current, so owners should track the annual date and book early, leaving time for repairs. A vehicle that passes earns a windshield sticker. One that fails gets a rejection notice that demands repair and a retest.

lines.text: Most gasoline cars: emissions plus safety.
Waiver after a repair attempt of four hundred fifty.

narration.text: Most gasoline cars take an emissions inspection along with the safety inspection, but motorcycles do not. Cars twenty-six or more model years old, cars under two model years old, and vehicles with historic registrations take the safety inspection only. If a car fails a high-enhanced or OBD II emissions inspection, it can get a waiver after a genuine repair attempt costing at least four hundred fifty dollars. So a failed emissions test is not the end of the road, but the waiver requires a real attempt to fix the problem first, at or above that cost.

lines.text: The DMV licenses dealers, stations, shops.
Then call or write the DMV.

narration.text: The DMV licenses dealers, inspection stations and repair shops. So before you do business with one, verify its credentials. If there is a problem, complain to the business's management first. If that does not settle it, call the DMV on weekdays between eight-thirty and four-fifteen, or write to the consumer box in Albany. Repair complaints are due within ninety days or three thousand miles, whichever comes first. So keep track of when the repair was done and how far you have driven since, because a complaint filed after those limits will be outside the window the manual gives.

lines.text: You moved here with a current certificate.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you moved to New York with a car whose inspection certificate from your old state is still current. How long does it last? Work it out before reading on. The answer is until it expires or for one year, whichever comes first. That is the mover's clock. If you had bought the car from an in-state dealer, the inspection would be needed within thirty days, and from a private seller, within ten days of registration. Three buyer kinds, three clocks, so always start by asking how the car came to you.

lines.text: Thirty, ten, or up to a year.
Verify, complain to management, then the DMV.

narration.text: To wrap up, in-state-sold vehicles need inspection within thirty days with a certificate before delivery, non-dealer buys need it within ten days of registration, and a mover keeps an existing certificate to expiry or one year, whichever first. Re-inspection is due before the certificate expires and on every registrant change. Failed high-enhanced or OBD II emissions tests can be waived after a genuine repair attempt of at least four hundred fifty dollars. Diesels face random roadside safety checks, and those over eighty-five hundred pounds add a diesel emissions inspection. Verify licensed businesses and complain to management first.
